docs.title: poincare-orchestra
docs.text:
Scenario-first LLM orchestration with geometry-aware memory. poincare-orchestra is the open-source reference implementation of the controller, ensemble and synthesis components of

D. Mojila, "LLM Orchestration with Geometry-Aware Memory," 2026 2nd International Conference on Big Data & Machine Learning (ICBDML), Bhopal, India, Feb. 2026, pp. 1–7. doi:10.1109/ICBDML68582.2026.11544690

It runs on top of poincare-memory, which implements the paper's memory component: a hierarchy-aware, time-aware store on the Poincaré ball.

Provenance. Written after the paper from its description. The system used for the paper's experiments is not released; every number this package reports is produced by the code here.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A use case is data, not code. A scenario bundles the domain hierarchy and dated facts that seed the memory, the specialist roles and their capability profiles, example tasks with the facets a good answer must cover, and the controller policy. The orchestrator is the same for every scenario; a new use case is a new JSON or YAML file. Three scenarios ship with the package, and everything runs offline with deterministic mock providers, so the control loop is inspectable and testable. Any real model can be plugged in through LiteLLM.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
• Readers of the paper who want to see the control loop of §III–§IV as small, rule-based, traceable steps rather than prose: each equation maps to a named function (see Paper mapping).
  • Engineers who need a transparent orchestration harness: deterministic providers for tests, a throttling detector and failover that can be exercised without a network, and a JSON trace of every run.
  • Students and teachers who want to write a scenario for their own domain in an afternoon (Scenarios).

docs.title: The eight steps of a run
docs.text: Orchestrator.run(question) analyses the question (intent, complexity, the memory branches and named entities it touches), decomposes it into sub-tasks along its clauses and branches with dependencies (eq. 5), matches each sub-task to a role by domain overlap and capability profile, allocates the budget by expected information gain per cost and skips what does not fit (eq. 6), retrieves hierarchy-aware context for each sub-task from the Poincaré memory (branch first, then named entities, then global), executes the sub-tasks through a provider-agnostic router whose throttling detector compares each response with the provider's own baseline and fails over with a cooldown, synthesises the responses by fusing near-duplicate claims and scoring coverage, density, agreement, recency and cost under the weighted-sum objective with epsilon constraints (eq. 7), and refines by re-investing the remaining budget in the weakest sub-tasks while a constraint fails. RunResult.explain() prints the whole trace; RunResult.to_json() serialises it.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install 'poincare-orchestra[yaml]'
poincare-orchestra list
poincare-orchestra run sprint_coaching "Athlete A reports recurring hamstring tightness after 400 m repeats. Plan the next two weeks."
poincare-orchestra eval support_kb

Continue with Getting started for a line-by-line reading of the output.

docs.title: controller
docs.text:
Metacognitive controller (paper §III-B, §III-C, §IV-B).

Four executive functions, each a small, inspectable step: 1. query analysis and intent recognition, with the memory hierarchy as the domain model; 2. hierarchical decomposition into coordinated sub-tasks Q -> {q_1..q_n} (eq. 5); 3. capability matching of sub-tasks to roles and profiles; 4. resource allocation by expected information gain per cost, I*(q_i) = argmax_I G(q_i, I) / C(I) (eq. 6), run as an investment cycle: invest, measure yield, re-invest the remainder.

The implementation is rule-based and offline so the control loop is transparent; an LLM-backed planner can replace decompose without touching the rest.

docs.title: Provider

Anything with a name and a complete(request) -> AgentResponse method.

docs.title: MockProvider
docs.text:
MockProvider(name: str, degrade_after: int | None = None, latency_s: float = 0.01, seed: int = 0, fail_after: int | None = None)

Deterministic provider that answers from the retrieved context.

It lets the whole orchestration run offline and in tests. degrade_after simulates a throttled commercial model: after that many calls, answers become truncated, slow and sometimes refused, which the detector should catch and the router should route around. fail_after simulates an outage: after that many calls every call raises RuntimeError.

docs.title: LiteLLMProvider
docs.text:
LiteLLMProvider(name: str, model: str, temperature: float = 0.2, max_tokens: int = 600, timeout_s: float | None = None, **kwargs: Any)

Any model LiteLLM can reach (pip install 'poincare-orchestra[litellm]').

model is a LiteLLM model string such as openai/gpt-4o-mini, anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5 or ollama/llama3; credentials come from the environment variables LiteLLM reads for that provider. The prompt asks for a JSON object {"answer": str, "claims": [{"text", "confidence", "sources"}]}; plain text is accepted as a fallback. timeout_s is passed to litellm.completion(timeout=...); a timeout raises and the router treats it like any other provider error (refused response, throttle event, failover). Extra keyword arguments go to litellm.completion unchanged.

docs.title: ThrottleDetector
docs.text:
ThrottleDetector(window: int = 6, min_history: int = 2, latency_factor: float = 3.0, length_ratio: float = 0.4, density_drop: float = 0.35)

Flags responses whose latency, length, density or refusal pattern breaks the provider's baseline.

The baseline is the provider's own recent responses (the last window that were not flagged); while a provider has fewer than min_history of them, the pooled responses of all providers stand in for it. A response is flagged when it is refused, when its latency exceeds latency_factor times the baseline median, when its token count is below length_ratio times the baseline median, or when its information density is more than density_drop below the baseline median. Flagged responses do not enter the baseline.

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
Router(providers: list[Provider], profiles: list[CapabilityProfile], detector: ThrottleDetector | None = None, cooldown_calls: int = 3)

Chooses a provider for each role by capability profile and health; fails over on throttling.

Candidates are ordered by: the profile's preferred provider first, then providers that are not cooling down, then the least loaded. A flagged response or a provider exception puts the provider in cooldown: it is skipped for the next cooldown_calls calls and the next candidate is tried; the last response is returned if every candidate fails. When every provider is cooling down they are tried anyway, least-degraded first, so a call never fails only because of cooldowns. call never raises on a provider exception: it is converted into a refused :class:AgentResponse and a :class:ThrottleEvent with reason error: <exception type>.

docs.title: Bundled scenarios
docs.text: poincare_orchestra.scenarios.sprint_coaching, poincare_orchestra.scenarios.clinical_anatomy and poincare_orchestra.scenarios.support_kb each expose a SCENARIO constant (a Scenario) built from module-level KNOWLEDGE, PROFILES, ROLES and TASKS lists. load_scenario(name) returns that constant; the same scenarios are exported as YAML under scenarios/ in the repository.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Sub-tasks carry a query_text used for retrieval and gain estimation, so the display-only "(focus: domain)" label no longer shifts the embedding of branch-scoped searches (the clinical-anatomy ACL task went from 0 to full facet recall).

First public release.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Scenario model and three bundled scenarios (sprint coaching, clinical anatomy, versioned support KB).
  • Scenario files: Scenario.from_file() / Scenario.to_file() / Scenario.to_dict() for JSON (always) and YAML (pip install 'poincare-orchestra[yaml]', with a clear ImportError otherwise); load_scenario() accepts a bundled name or a file path. The bundled scenarios are exported as scenarios/*.yaml, with a hand-written example scenarios/greenhouse.yaml.
  • Scenario validation with positional error messages: duplicate ids, parents declared after children or unknown, self-parents, duplicate profile/role names, roles referencing unknown profiles, tasks without facets, unknown objective or constraint names, thresholds outside [0, 1], malformed decay specs, empty lists. parse_decay(), OBJECTIVES and DECAY_KINDS are public.
  • Metacognitive controller: analysis, decomposition with dependencies, capability matching, investment scheduler with the skip rule and re-investment.
  • Ensemble: mock and LiteLLM providers, throttling detector, router with load balancing, cooldown and failover.
  • Router.call catches provider exceptions: they become a refused AgentResponse (provider error: ...) plus a ThrottleEvent with reason error: <type>, and trigger failover; Orchestrator.run never raises on a provider failure.
  • LiteLLMProvider(timeout_s=...) passes a per-call timeout to LiteLLM; parse_completion() and looks_like_refusal() are public and tested without network.
  • MockProvider(fail_after=N) simulates an outage.
  • Synthesis: claim fusion, five objectives, weighted sum with epsilon constraints, uncertainty, refinement loop.
  • RunResult.to_json() / RunResult.from_json() and EvalReport.to_json().
  • Module logger poincare_orchestra with INFO messages per pipeline stage (analyse, decompose, allocate, execute, synthesise, refine, eval), DEBUG details and WARNING on provider errors; a NullHandler is installed by default.
  • CLI: every command accepts a bundled name or a scenario path; new export and validate commands; run --json, run --fail-after, run --model NAME=MODEL, run --timeout, eval --json, global -v/-vv; exit code 1 for invalid scenarios in validate, 2 when a scenario cannot be loaded.
  • Evaluation harness (facet recall) and documentation site (mkdocs-material) at https://dhruvmojila.github.io/poincare-orchestra, with every code block executed by the test suite.

docs.title: Fixed (relative to the pre-release development version)
docs.text:
• Router.call raised AssertionError when every provider was in cooldown; all providers are now tried, least degraded first.
  • A provider in cooldown is skipped for exactly cooldown_calls calls (it was cooldown_calls - 1).

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
usage: poincare-orchestra [-h] [-v]
                          {list,run,eval,inspect,export,validate} ...

Scenario-first LLM orchestration with geometry-aware memory.

positional arguments:
  {list,run,eval,inspect,export,validate}
    list                list bundled scenarios
    run                 run one question through a scenario (offline mock
                        providers by default)
    eval                run a scenario's bundled tasks and report facet recall
    inspect             write the scenario memory's interactive HTML inspector
    export              write a scenario as a JSON or YAML file (a starting
                        point for your own)
    validate            load a scenario file and report problems

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -v, --verbose         log pipeline stages to stderr (-vv for debug)

Every command that takes a scenario accepts a bundled name (sprint_coaching, clinical_anatomy, support_kb) or the path of a .json, .yaml or .yml scenario file. Exit codes: 0 success, 1 when validate finds a problem, 2 when a scenario cannot be loaded or a flag is malformed (argparse uses 2 for usage errors too).

docs.title: list
docs.text:
poincare-orchestra list

clinical_anatomy   Clinical anatomy tutor — Hierarchical anatomy with clinical correlations and recent teaching cases.
sprint_coaching    400 m sprint coaching assistant — Physiology, biomechanics, strength and athlete records; dated observations decay with a 30-day half-life.
support_kb         Versioned support knowledge base — Facts with validity windows: superseded limits and requirements stop surfacing after their release date.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
usage: poincare-orchestra run [-h] [--degrade-after DEGRADE_AFTER]
                              [--fail-after FAIL_AFTER] [--model NAME=MODEL]
                              [--timeout TIMEOUT] [--json]
                              scenario question
Flag Effect --degrade-after N the first provider (alphabetically) starts returning truncated, slow and sometimes refused answers after N calls — exercises the throttling detector --fail-after N the first provider raises RuntimeError after N calls — exercises error handling and failover --model NAME=MODEL use a real model through LiteLLM for provider NAME (repeatable); NAME should match a provider in the scenario's profiles --timeout S per-call timeout in seconds for --model providers (passed to litellm.completion(timeout=...)) --json print RunResult.to_json() instead of RunResult.explain() 
poincare-orchestra run support_kb "What is the current API rate limit?"
poincare-orchestra run scenarios/greenhouse.yaml "What is the current standard feed?"
poincare-orchestra run support_kb "What is the current API rate limit?" --fail-after 0
poincare-orchestra run sprint_coaching "Athlete A shows forward trunk lean at the end of the race; explain the injury implication and then recommend a drill." --degrade-after 1
poincare-orchestra run support_kb "What is the current API rate limit?" --json

With real models (needs pip install 'poincare-orchestra[litellm]' and the provider's credentials in the environment; see Ensemble):

export OPENAI_API_KEY=...
poincare-orchestra run support_kb "What is the current API rate limit?" \
    --model provider-a=openai/gpt-4o-mini --model provider-b=ollama/llama3 --timeout 60

docs.title: eval
docs.text:
usage: poincare-orchestra eval [-h] [--json] scenario

Runs the scenario's bundled tasks and prints facet recall, mean J, the constraints-met rate and the number of throttle events, then one line per task. --json prints the EvalReport. Numbers for the bundled scenarios are in Evaluation.

poincare-orchestra eval clinical_anatomy
poincare-orchestra eval scenarios/support_kb.yaml --json

docs.title: inspect
docs.text:
usage: poincare-orchestra inspect [-h] [-o OUT] scenario

Writes the scenario memory as poincare-memory's self-contained interactive HTML inspector (Poincaré disk, table and tree). The default file name is <scenario name>.html.

poincare-orchestra inspect sprint_coaching
poincare-orchestra inspect scenarios/greenhouse.yaml -o greenhouse-memory.html

docs.title: export
docs.text:
usage: poincare-orchestra export [-h] [-o OUT] [--format {json,yaml}] scenario

Writes a scenario as JSON or YAML. The suffix of -o picks the format; without -o the scenario is printed to stdout (YAML unless --format json). Defaults and None fields are omitted, so the file states only what differs from the defaults. This is how the YAML files under scenarios/ are generated and the quickest way to start your own scenario:

poincare-orchestra export support_kb -o my_scenario.yaml
poincare-orchestra export clinical_anatomy --format json

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
usage: poincare-orchestra validate [-h] scenario

Loads a scenario and reports every problem at once: duplicate ids, parents declared after their children, unknown parents, roles that reference unknown profiles, tasks without facets, unknown objectives or constraints, malformed decay specs. Exit code 1 on problems.

poincare-orchestra validate scenarios/greenhouse.yaml

ok: greenhouse — 16 knowledge items, 2 profiles, 2 roles, 2 tasks, decay=half_life:720+validity

A broken file (a role pointing at a profile that does not exist) gives:

invalid: 1 validation error for Scenario
  Value error, roles[0] 'tier1': unknown profile 'ghost'; known profiles: ['tier2-model', 'tier1-model'] [type=value_error, ...]

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
-v prints INFO lines for each pipeline stage to stderr (analyse, decompose, allocate, execute, synthesise, refine, and eval per task); -vv adds DEBUG lines (retrieved record ids, role matching scores, per-provider answers). Provider errors are always printed as WARNING lines.

poincare-orchestra -vv run support_kb "Explain our encryption and retention defaults."

docs.title: Controller
docs.text: The metacognitive controller (paper §III-B, §III-C and §IV-B) has four executive functions: query analysis, hierarchical decomposition, capability matching and resource allocation. The implementation is rule-based and offline so that every decision is inspectable and testable; an LLM-backed planner can replace decompose without touching the rest (Replacing the planner).

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
analyze(query, memory, k=5) returns a QueryAnalysis with the intent, a complexity score, the memory branches and domains the question touches, the named entities, the retrieved record ids and the clauses.

Intent is the first matching pattern, in this order:

Intent Matched when the question contains planning plan, recommend, should, design, schedule, program, "next two/2/few weeks", "how do/can/should I/we" comparison compare, versus, vs, difference, better, rather than explanation why, explain, how does, mechanism, because factual none of the above

Clauses are split on ;, then, and then, and also, as well as, and sentence boundaries followed by a capital letter; fragments of three characters or fewer are dropped.

Branches and domains. Two searches of k results each run against the memory: one over structural records (those whose meta.kind is not in EPHEMERAL_KINDS = {event, ticket, issue, case, observation}) and one over the dated, ephemeral ones. Each hit, and each entity hit, is mapped to its branch: the ancestor one level below the root (branch_of). Roots themselves never count as a branch. The branch's meta.domain (or the text before its first colon) is the domain label.

Entities. entity_hits returns records with a parent whose leading phrase (the text before : or (, 2–24 characters) occurs in the lower-cased question. The convention "Athlete A: ...", "Ticket 4411: ...", "Release 2.4 (...)" in the scenario text is what makes this work.

Complexity is clip(0.15 · clauses + 0.12 · branches + 0.01 · words + 0.2 · [intent is planning], 0, 1).

from poincare_orchestra import analyze, load_scenario

scenario = load_scenario("support_kb")
memory = scenario.build_memory()
analysis = analyze(
    "Which Kafka version does the connector require now, and why might it fail after an upgrade?",
    memory,
    k=scenario.policy.retrieval_k,
)
print(analysis.intent, round(analysis.complexity, 2), analysis.domains, analysis.entity_ids)

explanation 0.91 ['storage', 'ingestion', 'api', 'tickets', 'releases'] []

docs.title: Decomposition (eq. 5)
docs.text:
The paper decomposes a query into coordinated sub-tasks:

\[Q \rightarrow \{q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_n\}\]

decompose(analysis, memory, roles, profiles, policy) builds the Plan:

  1. One facet sub-task per branch, phrased as the question plus (focus: <domain>) and carrying branch_id so that retrieval starts in that subtree.
  2. If the question has more than one clause, one clause sub-task per clause, each depending on the previous one (depends_on), so that "explain X and then recommend Y" runs in order.
  3. Duplicates (by lower-cased text) are dropped and the list is capped at policy.max_subtasks; a question that produced nothing becomes a single sub-task.
  4. Every sub-task carries the analysis' entity_ids so retrieval can look inside the named entities' subtrees.
from poincare_orchestra import ControllerPolicy, analyze, decompose, load_scenario

scenario = load_scenario("sprint_coaching")
memory = scenario.build_memory()
analysis = analyze(
    "Athlete A shows forward trunk lean at the end of the race; explain the injury implication and then recommend a drill.",
    memory,
)
print(analysis.intent, analysis.clauses)
roomy = ControllerPolicy(max_subtasks=6, total_budget=8.0)
plan = decompose(analysis, memory, scenario.roles, scenario.profiles, roomy)
for st in plan.subtasks:
    print(st.id, st.role, st.depends_on, st.question)

With the scenario's own max_subtasks=4 the plan stops after q4, which is what the bundled evaluation runs. Orchestrator.run executes sub-tasks whose dependencies are done first and falls back to the first pending one if a cycle ever appeared.

docs.title: Capability matching
docs.text:
Each sub-task goes to the role with the highest score

score(role) = |role.domains ∩ subtask.domains| + profile.fit(subtask.domains, intent)

where the role's CapabilityProfile contributes

fit = 0.6 · domain_score + 0.4 · intent_weight

with domain_score the share of the sub-task's domains the profile lists (0.5 when the sub-task has no domains) and intent_weight the profile's reasoning for planning and comparison, the mean of reasoning and creativity for explanation, and reliability for factual questions. The sub-task's cost is the profile's cost_per_call × (1 + complexity). This is the static side of the paper's capability matching; the dynamic side (provider health) lives in the Router.

docs.title: Investment scheduler (eq. 6)
docs.text:
The paper allocates resources to the investment with the best expected information gain per cost:

\[I^*(q_i) = \arg\max_{I} \frac{G(q_i, I)}{C(I)}\]

InvestmentScheduler instantiates the symbols as follows.

Expected gain \(G\): for each sub-task, relevance is the mean of \(e^{-d}\) over the top-3 hits of the sub-task question inside its branch subtree (globally if it has none; 0.1 with no hits), and novelty is one minus the highest cosine similarity between the sub-task question and the other sub-task questions (hashing embeddings, 128 dimensions). Then

G = clip(0.2 + 0.8 · relevance · (0.5 + 0.5 · novelty), 0.05, 1)

so a sub-task gains more when the memory holds relevant material and the sub-task is not a rephrasing of another.

Cost \(C\) is the sub-task cost from capability matching.

Allocation and the skip rule. Sub-tasks are sorted by \(G / C\). They are kept in that order while the sum of their costs fits policy.total_budget (the first one is always kept); the rest are marked skipped with budget 0 — the allocation decision of eq. 6 made explicit instead of overspending or under-funding everything. Each kept sub-task receives a floor of min(policy.min_budget, total_budget / kept) and the remainder is split in proportion to \(G / C\), so the budgets sum to total_budget.

from poincare_orchestra import InvestmentScheduler, analyze, decompose, load_scenario

scenario = load_scenario("support_kb")
memory = scenario.build_memory()
analysis = analyze(
    "Which Kafka version does the connector require now, and why might it fail after an upgrade?",
    memory,
    k=scenario.policy.retrieval_k,
)
plan = decompose(analysis, memory, scenario.roles, scenario.profiles, scenario.policy)
for st in plan.subtasks:
    print(st.id, st.role, st.domains, round(st.cost, 2))
allocation = InvestmentScheduler(scenario.policy).allocate(plan, memory)
print({k: round(v, 2) for k, v in allocation.items()}, [st.id for st in plan.subtasks if st.skipped])

q1 tier2 ['storage'] 2.29
q2 tier2 ['ingestion'] 2.29
q3 tier2 ['api'] 2.29
{'q2': 3.02, 'q1': 2.98} ['q3']

Each sub-task costs 1.2 × (1 + 0.91) = 2.29. Two fit the scenario's budget of 6.0 (4.58); the third would bring the total to 6.87, so it is skipped. The two kept sub-tasks get a floor of 0.5 each and share the remaining 5.0 almost equally, because their gains are nearly identical.

Yield and re-investment. After execution, measure_yield scores each response as distinct claims per 100 tokens (0 for refusals), and reinvest splits whatever budget is left equally over the lower-yielding half of the sub-tasks. Orchestrator.run uses this during refinement.

docs.title: Replacing the planner
docs.text: decompose returns a plain Plan: query, intent, complexity, domains, entities and a list of SubTasks with id, question, role, depends_on, domains, branch_id and entity_ids. Anything that produces such a plan — an LLM prompted with the memory's tree() and the role list, for example — can replace it; the scheduler, retrieval, router and synthesis consume the Plan and nothing else.

docs.title: Ensemble
docs.text: The provider-agnostic ensemble (paper §IV-D) executes sub-tasks: capability-profiled providers, a throttling detector that compares every response with the provider's own baseline, and a router that balances load, applies cooldowns and fails over.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text: A provider is anything with a name and a method complete(request: CompletionRequest) -> AgentResponse (the Provider protocol). The request carries the sub-task, the role name and system prompt, the retrieved context (texts, record ids and time weights) and the budget. The response is the paper's standardised schema: content, claims (text, confidence, source record ids), confidence, sources, latency_s, tokens, refused and a free meta dict.

docs.title: MockProvider
docs.text:
MockProvider(name, degrade_after=None, latency_s=0.01, seed=0, fail_after=None) answers deterministically from the context: it turns the first min(len(context), 3 + 2 · budget) records into claims with confidence 0.95 − 0.07 · rank and writes a bullet list. It is the default provider everywhere and what the test suite and the bundled evaluation use.

  • degrade_after=N: after N calls the provider behaves like a throttled commercial model — six times the latency and, with probability 0.4 (seeded), a refusal, otherwise an answer cut to a fifth with a single claim.
  • fail_after=N: after N calls every call raises RuntimeError, simulating an outage.

On the command line these are --degrade-after and --fail-after, applied to the alphabetically first provider.

docs.title: LiteLLMProvider
docs.text:
LiteLLMProvider(name, model, temperature=0.2, max_tokens=600, timeout_s=None, **kwargs) reaches any model LiteLLM supports (pip install 'poincare-orchestra[litellm]'). The prompt sends the context records with their ids and asks for a JSON object {"answer": ..., "claims": [{"text", "confidence", "sources"}]}; parse_completion extracts it from the reply (code fences and surrounding prose are tolerated, malformed claims are skipped) and falls back to plain text with no claims. Short replies of the form "I cannot/can't/am unable to help|assist|comply" are marked refused. Token counts come from the provider's usage report when present.

timeout_s is passed to litellm.completion(timeout=...); a timeout raises inside the provider and the router handles it like any other exception (below). Extra keyword arguments (api_base, api_key, …) go to litellm.completion unchanged.

Credentials and model names follow LiteLLM's conventions:

Provider Credentials Example model string OpenAI OPENAI_API_KEY openai/gpt-4o-mini Anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5 Ollama (local) none; the server listens on http://localhost:11434 by default, override with api_base= or OLLAMA_API_BASE ollama/llama3

Model ids change over time; the current list is in LiteLLM's provider documentation.

from poincare_orchestra import LiteLLMProvider, Orchestrator, load_scenario

scenario = load_scenario("support_kb")
providers = [
    LiteLLMProvider("provider-a", "openai/gpt-4o-mini", timeout_s=60),
    LiteLLMProvider("provider-b", "ollama/llama3", api_base="http://localhost:11434"),
]
print(Orchestrator(scenario, providers=providers).run("What is the current API rate limit?").explain())

Provider names should match the provider field of the scenario's capability profiles (provider-a, provider-b in the bundled scenarios); the router prefers the profile's provider and load-balances across the others. If a profile names a provider that was not given, a warning is logged and its roles are routed to whatever is available.

docs.title: Capability profiles
docs.text: A CapabilityProfile describes a model statically: domains, reasoning, creativity, reliability, cost_per_call, latency_s and the provider it runs on. The controller uses profiles twice — to match roles to sub-tasks and to price them (Controller) — and the router uses provider as the preferred route for each role. The dynamic performance characteristics the paper mentions are the detector's and router's state: recent latencies, lengths, densities, refusals and cooldowns.

docs.title: Throttling detector
docs.text:
ThrottleDetector.observe(response) returns a ThrottleEvent when a response breaks the provider's baseline, or None and adds the response to the baseline. The baseline is the provider's own last window unflagged responses; while a provider has fewer than min_history of them, the pooled unflagged responses of all providers stand in, so detection works from the second call of a run.

Signal Fires when Default threshold refusal the response is marked refused — latency latency_s exceeds latency_factor × the baseline median latency latency_factor=3.0 length tokens is below length_ratio × the baseline median token count length_ratio=0.4 density the unique-token ratio of the content is more than density_drop below the baseline median density_drop=0.35

Defaults: window=6, min_history=2. Flagged responses never enter the baseline, so one bad answer does not lower the bar for the next.

from poincare_orchestra import AgentResponse, ThrottleDetector

detector = ThrottleDetector()


def response(content: str, latency_s: float, refused: bool = False) -> AgentResponse:
    return AgentResponse(
        subtask_id="q1",
        role="tier2",
        provider="provider-a",
        content=content,
        latency_s=latency_s,
        tokens=len(content.split()),
        refused=refused,
    )


normal = "The API rate limit is 250 requests per second per project since release 2.4, with bursts up to 500 for 10 seconds."
for _ in range(3):
    print(detector.observe(response(normal, 0.8)))  # builds the baseline
print(detector.observe(response(normal, 3.0)))  # slow
print(detector.observe(response("Rate limit: 250.", 0.8)))  # short
print(detector.observe(response("limit " * 20, 0.8)))  # repetitive
print(detector.observe(response("I am unable to help with this request.", 0.8, refused=True)))
print(detector.observe(response(normal, 0.9)))  # back to normal

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
Router(providers, profiles, detector=None, cooldown_calls=3) chooses a provider per call:

  1. Candidate order: the profile's preferred provider first, then providers that are not cooling down, then the least loaded (load counts attempted calls).
  2. Detection: every response goes through the detector. An unflagged response is returned.
  3. Cooldown and failover: a flagged response puts the provider in cooldown — it is skipped for the next cooldown_calls router calls — and the next candidate is tried. If every candidate is flagged, the last response is returned (never an exception).
  4. Provider exceptions: if complete() raises, the router catches the exception, builds a refused AgentResponse whose content is provider error: <Type>: <message> (the error is also in meta["error"]), records a ThrottleEvent with reason error: <Type>, puts the provider in cooldown and fails over exactly as for a flagged response. Orchestrator.run therefore never raises because of a provider.
  5. All providers cooling down: they are tried anyway, least-degraded first, so a call is never refused merely because of cooldowns.

router.events lists every throttle event, router.degraded the remaining cooldown per provider, and each flagged response carries meta["throttle"] with the reasons.

from poincare_orchestra import CapabilityProfile, CompletionRequest, MockProvider, Router, SubTask

request = CompletionRequest(
    subtask=SubTask(id="q1", question="What is the current API rate limit?"),
    role_name="tier2",
    system_prompt="You are tier-2 support.",
    context=["API rate limit is 250 requests per second per project since release 2.4"],
    context_ids=["rate_new"],
    budget=1.0,
)
router = Router(
    [MockProvider("provider-a", fail_after=0, latency_s=0.0), MockProvider("provider-b", latency_s=0.0)],
    [CapabilityProfile(name="tier2-model", provider="provider-a")],
)
for _ in range(5):
    answer = router.call(request, "tier2-model")
    print(answer.provider, answer.refused, dict(router.degraded))
print([event.reasons for event in router.events])

docs.title: Throttling inside a run
docs.text:
--degrade-after 1 makes provider-a degrade from its second call. In this four-sub-task question q1 and q4 both prefer provider-a; the baseline after two responses (one per provider) is enough for the detector to flag q4's truncated, slow reply on two signals, and the router fails over to provider-b:

poincare-orchestra run sprint_coaching "Athlete A shows forward trunk lean at the end of the race; explain the injury implication and then recommend a drill." --degrade-after 1

Over several runs on the same Orchestrator the baseline persists and later degradations are caught.

docs.title: The harness
docs.text:
Orchestrator.evaluate() runs every Task of the scenario through run() on the same orchestrator (so the router's history and cooldowns carry over between tasks, as they would in service) and returns an EvalReport:

Field Meaning facet_recall mean over tasks of facets found / facets expected. A facet is found when it occurs, case-insensitively, as a substring of the synthesised answer or of any provider response of that run mean_weighted_score mean of the synthesis objective J (eq. 7) over tasks constraints_met_rate share of tasks whose final synthesis satisfied every epsilon constraint throttle_events number of throttle events (including error: <type> events) recorded by the router over the whole evaluation per_task per task: question, facet_recall, missing facets, J, number of subtasks

Facet recall is deliberately simple: it measures whether the right records reached the answer, which is what the controller, the retrieval and the synthesis are responsible for. It does not judge wording, and with mock providers it cannot judge reasoning. It is not the paper's evaluation (expert ratings, bits per token, response time; see Paper mapping).

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
poincare-orchestra eval support_kb
poincare-orchestra eval scenarios/greenhouse.yaml
poincare-orchestra eval sprint_coaching --json

or in Python:

from poincare_orchestra import Orchestrator, load_scenario

report = Orchestrator(load_scenario("support_kb")).evaluate()
print(report.summary())
for row in report.per_task:
    print(row["facet_recall"], row["missing"], row["question"])

EvalReport.to_json() serialises the report; EvalReport.model_validate_json() restores it.

docs.title: Adding tasks
docs.text:
A task is a question plus the facets a good answer must contain:

tasks:
- question: Which Kafka version does the connector require now, and why might it fail after an upgrade?
  expected_facets: [Kafka 3.0, "4530"]
  notes: the second facet is the ticket id that explains the failure

Facets should be short, distinctive substrings of the records you expect to be cited (version numbers, ids, technical terms). Validation rejects tasks with no facets or with blank facets, so every task is measurable. In Python, Task(question=..., expected_facets=[...]) goes in Scenario.tasks.

docs.title: Why retrieval uses query_text
docs.text:
Each sub-task carries two strings: question, the labelled form shown in traces (for example with a "(focus: musculoskeletal)" suffix), and query_text, the clean question or clause. Branch-scoped retrieval and the gain estimate always embed query_text. With a character-n-gram embedder a presentation suffix is enough to reorder a branch's records, and the mock provider only quotes the top of its context, so letting the label leak into the query would cost recall on specific records such as acl in clinical_anatomy. The rule generalises to any embedder: keep presentation text out of the retrieval query. The embedder itself still matters for ranking, and you can swap it per scenario:

from poincare_memory import HashingEmbedder

from poincare_orchestra import Orchestrator, load_scenario

scenario = load_scenario("clinical_anatomy")
memory = scenario.build_memory(embedder=HashingEmbedder(dim=512))  # any Embedder works here
report = Orchestrator(scenario, memory=memory).evaluate()
print(report.summary())

poincare-memory also provides SentenceTransformerEmbedder for dense embeddings (pip install 'poincare-memory[embed]'), which is the realistic choice outside tests.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
• MockProvider output depends only on the request and on its seed (the seed drives the refusal choice when degraded).
  • Latencies are real measurements; the detector's latency signal fires at 3× the baseline median, which a 10 ms sleep clears comfortably on an idle machine.
  • clock= on Orchestrator/Scenario.build_memory() fixes "now" for the relative dates; by default it is the time of the run, and days_ago offsets keep every relative age constant, so time weights do not drift between runs.

docs.title: Is this the paper's experimental system?
docs.text: No. It is a reference implementation written after the paper from its description. The system used for the experiments in §V of the paper is not released, and this package does not reproduce Table I of the paper. Every number in this documentation comes from running this code on the bundled scenarios (Evaluation).

docs.title: Where do the equations come from?
docs.text: From the paper: eq. 5 (decomposition), eq. 6 (investment) and eq. 7 (weighted sum with epsilon constraints) are quoted in Paper mapping. The instantiation of their symbols (what counts as information gain, how coverage is measured) is this package's choice and is documented on the Controller and Synthesis pages.

docs.title: Why are the mock providers so simple?
docs.text: So that the control loop can be observed in isolation. MockProvider answers from the retrieved context deterministically, can be told to degrade (truncation, slowness, refusals) or to fail after N calls, and runs in milliseconds. Capability matching, budget allocation, throttling detection, failover, synthesis and refinement all run exactly as they would with real models.

docs.title: Can I use real models?
docs.text: Yes, through LiteLLM: pip install 'poincare-orchestra[litellm]', then pass LiteLLMProvider instances or use poincare-orchestra run ... --model provider-a=openai/gpt-4o-mini. Provider names should match the provider field of the scenario's capability profiles. See Ensemble.

docs.title: Why did a sub-task get SKIPPED (budget)?
docs.text: The investment scheduler keeps sub-tasks in order of expected gain per cost while their summed cost fits policy.total_budget (the first one is always kept). The rest are skipped rather than under-funded, and they are listed as "Open sub-questions" in the answer. Raise total_budget, lower max_subtasks, or give the roles cheaper profiles. Details in Controller.

docs.title: What happens when a provider fails or times out?
docs.text: Router.call catches the exception, records a refused AgentResponse whose content starts with provider error:, appends a ThrottleEvent with reason error: <ExceptionType>, puts the provider in cooldown and tries the next candidate. Orchestrator.run therefore never raises because of a provider; if every provider fails, the run completes with refused responses and uncertainty = 1.0.

docs.title: Why is facet recall on clinical_anatomy not 1.0?
docs.text: All bundled tasks score full facet recall with the offline mock providers; the numbers are reported as measured in Evaluation, which also explains why retrieval embeds the clean query_text rather than the labelled sub-task.

docs.title: Does it need a GPU or network access?
docs.text: No. The default embedder is poincare_memory.HashingEmbedder (pure NumPy), the default providers are offline mocks, and the test suite runs without network. Real models need whatever LiteLLM needs for the chosen provider.

docs.title: Is the retrieval really hyperbolic?
docs.text: The memory is poincare_memory.Memory: every record is a point in the Poincaré ball, with depth from its level in the hierarchy you declare with parent. This package uses its subtree searches (a sub-task's branch, then the entities the question names), its time weights (decay policies and validity windows) and its inspect() visualiser. The geometry itself is documented in poincare-memory.

docs.title: How do I write a scenario for my domain?
docs.text: Export a bundled one as a starting point (poincare-orchestra export support_kb -o mine.yaml), edit it, poincare-orchestra validate mine.yaml, then run and eval it. A complete annotated example is in Scenarios.

docs.title: Can I replace the rule-based controller with an LLM planner?
docs.text: Yes. decompose returns a Plan; anything that produces a Plan with SubTasks (ids, questions, domains, branch_id, depends_on) can replace it, and the scheduler, router and synthesis keep working unchanged.

docs.title: Why do results vary slightly between runs?
docs.text: Mock responses are deterministic, but latencies are measured with a real clock. The throttling detector compares latencies with a median, so on a heavily loaded machine a spurious latency event is possible; the bundled evaluations report throttle events 0 on an idle machine.

docs.title: How should I cite it?
docs.text: Cite the paper (see Home). The software metadata is in CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json in the repository.

docs.title: Reading the trace line by line
docs.text:
Question: — the question as asked.

Intent: planning complexity=1.00 domains=[...] entities=[...] — the output of query analysis (Controller › Analysis). The intent is one of planning, comparison, explanation or factual; here the word Plan matched the planning pattern. Complexity is a clipped linear score of clause count, branch count, word count and intent, so a long planning question saturates at 1.00. Domains are the labels of the memory branches the question touches (the branch's meta.domain), in retrieval order. Entities are records whose leading phrase appears in the question: both athlete_a ("Athlete A: 400 m personal best…") and a_better ("Athlete A: hamstring flexibility improved…") begin with "Athlete A".

[q1] role=strength_coach gain=0.32 cost=1.20 budget=3.18 … (focus: strength) — one line per sub-task of the plan (eq. 5). The controller made one facet sub-task per domain branch; questions with several clauses also get clause sub-tasks that depend on each other (after ['q1']). role is the matched role (domain overlap plus the capability profile's fit for the intent). cost is the profile's cost_per_call × (1 + complexity): 0.6 × 2 = 1.20 for the fast-specialist profile and 1.5 × 2 = 3.00 for deep-reasoner. gain is the expected information gain (relevance of what the memory holds × novelty against the other sub-tasks) and budget the share of policy.total_budget allocated by gain per cost (eq. 6).

SKIPPED (budget) — q4 did not fit: the first three cost 1.20 + 1.20 + 3.00 = 5.40 and adding 3.00 would exceed the scenario's budget of 8.0, so it is skipped rather than under-funded and shows up later as an open sub-question.

<- q1 via provider-b (0.01s, 201 tok, conf 0.67) — one line per response: which provider the router chose (the fast-specialist profile prefers provider-b), latency, token count and the mean confidence of the response's claims. A refused response carries the flag REFUSED.

!! throttling on provider-a: … — printed for every throttle event: a response that broke the provider's baseline (refusal, latency, length or density) or a provider exception (error: <type>). None occurred here; Ensemble shows runs that have them.

Scores: coverage=0.75, density=1.00, agreement=0.07, recency=0.93, cost=0.32 J=0.695 … — the five objectives of the synthesis (Synthesis › Objectives): 3 of 4 sub-tasks answered gives coverage 0.75; density is claims per 60 tokens, clipped to 1; agreement is the mean pairwise overlap of cited sources between responses (the three responses cited mostly different records); recency is the mean time weight of the cited records (dated observations decay with the scenario's 30-day half-life); cost is 1 − spent/budget = 1 − 5.40/8.0. J is the weighted sum of eq. 7 with the policy's weights (0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.15, 0.15): 0.4·0.75 + 0.2·1.00 + 0.1·0.07 + 0.15·0.93 + 0.15·0.32 ≈ 0.695. constraints_met=True means every epsilon constraint held (by default coverage ≥ 0.5 and density ≥ 0.2), so no refinement round ran (refinements=0). uncertainty falls with claim confidence and rises with refusals.

Answer: — the composed answer: which roles contributed, the fused claims sorted by confidence with the ids of the memory records that support them, and the open sub-questions that were skipped or unanswered.

docs.title: The same from Python
docs.text:
from poincare_orchestra import Orchestrator, load_scenario

scenario = load_scenario("sprint_coaching")
orchestrator = Orchestrator(scenario)  # offline mock providers, one per provider name in the profiles
result = orchestrator.run("Is Athlete B ready to resume plyometrics?")

RunResult is a Pydantic model, so every part of the trace is data:

for st in result.plan.subtasks:
    print(st.id, st.role, round(st.expected_gain, 2), round(st.budget, 2), st.skipped)
print(result.synthesis.objective_scores)
print(round(result.synthesis.weighted_score, 3), result.synthesis.constraints_met)
print([claim.text for claim in result.synthesis.claims][:2])
print(result.trace)  # the controller's own log of what it decided

Serialise and restore a run (the JSON contains the plan, every response, the synthesis, the allocations, the throttle events and the trace):

from poincare_orchestra import RunResult

text = result.to_json()
assert RunResult.from_json(text) == result

Paper What it says Where it lives here §I Introduction, §II Related Work Motivation and context Home, FAQ §III-A Geometric Knowledge Representation (eq. 1–3) Poincaré ball, metric tensor, hyperbolic distance poincare-memory; used through Scenario.build_memory() and Memory.search(mode="subtree") §III-B Metacognitive Control Theory (eq. 4) Control signal C(t) = F(M(t), G(t), R(t)) Orchestrator.run: state = plan and responses, goal = constraints, resources = ControllerPolicy.total_budget §III-B (eq. 5) Hierarchical decomposition Q → {q_1, …, q_n} controller.decompose → Plan.subtasks with depends_on (Controller) §III-C Information-Theoretic Resource Allocation (eq. 6) I*(q_i) = argmax_I G(q_i, I) / C(I) InvestmentScheduler.expected_gain, .allocate (skip rule), .measure_yield, .reinvest (Controller) §III-D Multi-Objective Response Optimization (eq. 7) max J(R) = Σ w_i f_i(R) s.t. f_j(R) ≥ ε_j synthesis.weighted_sum; Orchestrator._context retrieval order §IV-D Provider-Agnostic LLM Ensemble: capability profiling Domain expertise, reasoning, creativity, reliability CapabilityProfile fields of the same names §IV-D: throttling detection and mitigation Response patterns, computation time, information density ThrottleDetector signals: refusal, latency, length, density (Ensemble) §IV-D: response standardization One schema for every model output schema.AgentResponse, schema.Claim §IV-D: load balancing and failover Balance across models, fail over on degradation Router: candidate order, cooldown, failover, provider-exception handling §IV-E Response Synthesis: multi-source integration Fuse partial results synthesis.fuse_claims §IV-E: quality assessment Multiple quality dimensions the five objectives in synthesis.score_objectives §IV-E: uncertainty quantification Calibrated uncertainty estimates SynthesisResult.uncertainty (a proxy, see Synthesis) §IV-E: iterative refinement Re-process when thresholds fail the refinement loop in Orchestrator.run (refine_rounds) §V Experimental Evaluation, Table I Expert-rated accuracy, bits/token, response time, satisfaction Not reproduced. docs.title: Equations as quoted in the paper
docs.text:
Eq. 5 (hierarchical decomposition):

\[Q \rightarrow \{q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_n\}\]

Eq. 6 (optimal investment per sub-task):

\[I^*(q_i) = \arg\max_{I} \frac{G(q_i, I)}{C(I)}\]

Eq. 7 (weighted sum with epsilon constraints):

\[\max_{R}\; J(R) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} w_i f_i(R) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad f_j(R) \geq \epsilon_j,\ \forall j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, m\}\]

The controller and synthesis pages show how each symbol is instantiated in code.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: A scenario is a complete use case as data. The orchestrator never changes; the scenario decides what the memory holds, who answers, what a good answer contains and how much it may cost.

docs.title: Anatomy of a scenario
docs.text:
Field Type Role name string identifier; also the default file name for inspect title, description string shown by poincare-orchestra list knowledge list of KnowledgeItem the hierarchy and dated facts that seed the memory profiles list of CapabilityProfile what each model/provider is good at and what it costs roles list of AgentRole the specialists; each points at a profile tasks list of Task example questions with the facets a good answer must contain policy ControllerPolicy budget, retrieval depth, objective weights, constraints, temporal policy

A Scenario validates itself on construction and when loaded from a file. Problems are reported together with their position: duplicate knowledge ids, a parent declared after its child or not at all, an item that is its own parent, duplicate profile or role names, a role that references an unknown profile, a task without facets or with a blank facet, unknown objective names in the policy, thresholds outside [0, 1], malformed decay specs, and empty knowledge, profiles or roles lists.

docs.title: Knowledge: the hierarchy and its dates
docs.text:
KnowledgeItem field Meaning id unique id; cited by claims and shown in answers text the record. Begin entity records with the entity name and a colon ("Athlete A: ...", "Ticket 4411: ..."): the controller recognises a question that names them parent id of the parent record, which must be declared earlier in the list. This builds the hierarchy that becomes depth on the Poincaré ball days_ago age of a dated record; undated items are structural knowledge and count as current valid_from_days_ago, valid_until_days_ago a validity window, enforced by the validity decay kind: superseded facts stop surfacing after their end date meta free dict. Two keys matter: domain on a branch (a child of the root) labels the domain the controller reports; kind in event, ticket, issue, case, observation marks a dated, ephemeral record

Shape the hierarchy as root → domain branches → facts → dated observations. The controller maps every retrieved record to its branch, so the branches are the domains it reasons about; the retrieval searches a sub-task's branch first, then the subtrees of the entities the question names, then the whole memory. Records whose time weight has decayed below 0.001 (expired validity windows, very old observations under a short half-life) are not retrieved.

All dates are relative, so a scenario never goes stale: Scenario.build_memory(now=...) anchors them (default: the time of the run).

docs.title: Roles and capability profiles
docs.text:
CapabilityProfile field Default Used for name — referenced by roles provider — the provider the router prefers for this profile; match it to your provider objects' names domains [] domain labels the model is good at reasoning, creativity, reliability 0.5 each intent-dependent fit: planning and comparison weigh reasoning, explanation the mean of reasoning and creativity, factual reliability cost_per_call 1.0 sub-task cost = cost_per_call × (1 + complexity) latency_s 1.0 descriptive (the detector measures real latencies)

An AgentRole has a name, a description, the system_prompt sent to the provider, the domains it covers and the profile it runs on. Capability matching scores roles by domain overlap plus profile fit (Controller). Give each domain branch at least one role that lists it.

docs.title: Tasks and facets
docs.text: A Task is a question, the expected_facets (substrings a good answer must contain, case-insensitive) and optional notes. Tasks drive poincare-orchestra eval and should be answerable from the records: a facet is usually a version number, an id or a technical term that appears in the record you expect to be cited (Evaluation).

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
ControllerPolicy field Default Effect max_subtasks 4 cap on the plan size total_budget 6.0 the budget split by gain per cost; sub-tasks that do not fit are skipped min_budget 0.5 floor per kept sub-task (reduced when the budget is small) retrieval_k 5 base number of records retrieved per sub-task (scaled by its budget, up to 2×) objectives coverage 0.4, density 0.2, agreement 0.1, recency 0.15, cost 0.15 the weights \(w_i\) of eq. 7 constraints coverage ≥ 0.5, density ≥ 0.2 the thresholds \(\epsilon_j\) of eq. 7 refine_rounds 1 refinement rounds allowed while a constraint fails decay half_life:720 temporal policy of the memory (below)

The decay spec grammar: none · half_life:<hours> (default 720 h = 30 days) · ebbinghaus:<hours> (stability, default 168 h) · validity (validity windows) · any of these joined with + for a product, e.g. half_life:2160+validity. parse_decay() turns a spec into a poincare_memory policy.

from poincare_orchestra import ControllerPolicy, parse_decay

print(ControllerPolicy().model_dump())
print(parse_decay("half_life:2160+validity"))

docs.title: Writing your own scenario in YAML
docs.text:
This is scenarios/greenhouse.yaml from the repository, a complete scenario for a small tomato greenhouse. Every feature appears once: a hierarchy with labelled branches, a superseded record hidden by a validity window, dated observations, an entity (Bay 3), two profiles on two providers, two roles, two measurable tasks and a policy.

# A complete hand-written scenario. Everything the orchestrator needs is in this file:
# the knowledge hierarchy (parents before children), dated and versioned records,
# capability profiles, roles, example tasks with facets, and the controller policy.
name: greenhouse
title: Greenhouse crop advisor
description: Climate, pest and crop knowledge for a small tomato greenhouse, with dated scouting notes.
knowledge:
- id: greenhouse
  text: Greenhouse operations knowledge base for tomatoes and cucumbers
  meta: {domain: operations}
- id: climate
  text: "Climate: temperature, humidity and ventilation targets"
  parent: greenhouse
  meta: {domain: climate}          # a branch label; analysis reports it as a domain
- id: temp
  text: Tomatoes set fruit best between 18 and 26 °C; above 32 °C pollen viability drops sharply
  parent: climate
- id: humidity
  text: Keep relative humidity below 85% at night to limit botrytis and leaf mould
  parent: climate
- id: venting
  text: Open roof vents when the canopy exceeds 24 °C; a 2 °C day-night difference improves fruit set
  parent: climate
- id: pests
  text: "Pests and diseases: identification and thresholds"
  parent: greenhouse
  meta: {domain: pests}
- id: whitefly
  text: Whitefly adults sit on the underside of young leaves; treat when counts exceed 5 per leaf
  parent: pests
- id: encarsia
  text: Encarsia formosa parasitises whitefly nymphs; release weekly at 3 per square metre while counts rise
  parent: pests
- id: botrytis
  text: Botrytis (grey mould) starts on pruning wounds in humid nights; prune in the morning so wounds dry
  parent: pests
- id: crops
  text: "Crops: varieties and feeding"
  parent: greenhouse
  meta: {domain: crops}
- id: feed_old
  text: Standard feed is EC 2.2 with potassium raised at fruit set (2025 schedule)
  parent: crops
  days_ago: 400
  valid_until_days_ago: 60         # superseded: hidden by the validity policy
  meta: {version: "2025"}
- id: feed_new
  text: Standard feed is EC 2.5 with calcium raised in hot weeks (2026 schedule)
  parent: crops
  days_ago: 60
  valid_from_days_ago: 60
  meta: {version: "2026"}
- id: bays
  text: Scouting notes per bay
  parent: greenhouse
  meta: {domain: scouting}
- id: bay3
  text: "Bay 3: tomato, variety Merlice, planted in week 4"   # "Bay 3" is an entity
  parent: bays
- id: bay3_whitefly
  text: "Bay 3: whitefly at 8 adults per leaf on the south row"
  parent: bay3
  days_ago: 2
  meta: {kind: observation}        # dated kinds: event, ticket, issue, case, observation
- id: bay3_humidity
  text: "Bay 3: night humidity logged at 90% for three nights"
  parent: bay3
  days_ago: 1
  meta: {kind: observation}
profiles:
- name: agronomist-model
  provider: provider-a             # the provider name a router looks for
  domains: [climate, pests, crops]
  reasoning: 0.85
  reliability: 0.8
  cost_per_call: 1.2
  latency_s: 1.5
- name: scout-model
  provider: provider-b
  domains: [scouting, operations]
  reasoning: 0.6
  reliability: 0.9
  cost_per_call: 0.5
  latency_s: 0.5
roles:
- name: agronomist
  description: Crop and climate agronomist
  system_prompt: You are a greenhouse agronomist. Answer from the records; cite record ids.
  domains: [climate, pests, crops]
  profile: agronomist-model
- name: scout
  description: Pest scout
  system_prompt: You summarise scouting notes with their dates; cite record ids.
  domains: [scouting]
  profile: scout-model
tasks:
- question: Bay 3 shows whitefly and humid nights; what should we do this week?
  expected_facets: [Encarsia, humidity]
- question: What is the current standard feed?
  expected_facets: [EC 2.5]
policy:
  max_subtasks: 3
  total_budget: 6.0                # 5.0 would skip the third sub-task of the first task (see the docs)
  decay: half_life:720+validity    # 30-day half-life for dated records, validity windows enforced
  constraints: {coverage: 0.5}

Check it, evaluate it and ask it something:

poincare-orchestra validate scenarios/greenhouse.yaml
poincare-orchestra eval scenarios/greenhouse.yaml
poincare-orchestra run scenarios/greenhouse.yaml "What is the current standard feed?"

ok: greenhouse — 16 knowledge items, 2 profiles, 2 roles, 2 tasks, decay=half_life:720+validity
greenhouse: 2 tasks, facet recall 1.00, mean J 0.746, constraints met 100%, throttle events 0
  recall=1.00 J=0.778 subtasks=3 missing=[]  Bay 3 shows whitefly and humid nights; what should we do this week?
  recall=1.00 J=0.713 subtasks=3 missing=[]  What is the current standard feed?

The feed question is answered from feed_new only: feed_old carries valid_until_days_ago: 60, so under the validity policy its time weight is zero and it is never retrieved.

docs.title: The budget decides what gets investigated
docs.text:
The first task touches three branches (climate, scouting, pests), and the two agronomist sub-tasks cost 2.39 each. With total_budget: 6.0 all three sub-tasks fit (5.77) and the answer includes the encarsia record; with 5.0 the pests sub-task is skipped and the Encarsia facet is missed. You can see the skip rule from Python without editing the file:

from poincare_orchestra import Orchestrator, Scenario

scenario = Scenario.from_file("scenarios/greenhouse.yaml")
question = "Bay 3 shows whitefly and humid nights; what should we do this week?"
for budget in (5.0, 6.0):

    print(

        [(st.id, st.domains[0], st.skipped) for st in result.plan.subtasks],
        "Encarsia" in result.synthesis.answer,
    )

docs.title: Starting from a bundled scenario
docs.text: poincare-orchestra export support_kb -o my_scenario.yaml writes a bundled scenario as YAML (JSON with a .json suffix) with defaults omitted. Edit it, then validate, run and eval it by path. YAML needs pip install 'poincare-orchestra[yaml]'; JSON always works.

docs.title: Loading and saving from Python
docs.text:
from poincare_orchestra import Scenario, load_scenario

scenario = load_scenario("scenarios/greenhouse.yaml")  # bundled name or path
assert scenario == Scenario.from_file("scenarios/greenhouse.yaml")

path = scenario.to_file("my_copy.json")  # format follows the suffix; format="yaml" overrides
assert Scenario.from_file(path) == scenario
data = scenario.to_dict()  # JSON-compatible dict, defaults and None omitted
assert Scenario.model_validate(data) == scenario

A scenario built in Python (as the bundled ones are, see src/poincare_orchestra/scenarios/support_kb.py) is passed straight to Orchestrator(scenario).

docs.title: Synthesis
docs.text: Response synthesis (paper §III-D and §IV-E) turns the sub-task responses into one answer and decides whether it is good enough. synthesize() does four things: fuse claims, score five objectives, apply the weighted-sum objective with epsilon constraints (eq. 7), and estimate uncertainty. Orchestrator.run then refines while a constraint fails and budget remains.

docs.title: Claim fusion
docs.text:
Every non-refused response contributes its Claims. Claims are embedded with the same offline HashingEmbedder (128 dimensions) and merged greedily: a claim joins an existing fused claim when the cosine similarity of their embeddings is at least merge_threshold (default 0.85). The fused claim keeps the first text, the maximum confidence, and the union of the sources (sorted). Fused claims are sorted by confidence, then text.

from poincare_orchestra import AgentResponse, Claim, fuse_claims

responses = [
    AgentResponse(
        subtask_id="q1",
        role="tier2",
        provider="provider-a",
        content="The limit is 250 requests per second.",
        tokens=30,
        sources=["rate_new"],
        claims=[
            Claim(text="API rate limit is 250 requests per second", confidence=0.9, sources=["rate_new"]),
        ],
    ),
    AgentResponse(
        subtask_id="q2",
        role="tier1",
        provider="provider-b",
        content="250 rps per project; tokens expire after 60 minutes.",
        tokens=30,
        sources=["rate_new", "rel24", "auth"],
        claims=[
            Claim(
                text="API rate limit is 250 requests per second per project",
                confidence=0.7,
                sources=["rate_new", "rel24"],
            ),
            Claim(text="Tokens expire after 60 minutes", confidence=0.8, sources=["auth"]),
        ],
    ),
]
for claim in fuse_claims(responses):
    print(claim.confidence, claim.sources, claim.text)

0.9 ['rate_new', 'rel24'] API rate limit is 250 requests per second
0.8 ['auth'] Tokens expire after 60 minutes

The two rate-limit claims differ by two words and merge; the merged claim carries both providers' sources.

docs.title: The five objectives
docs.text:
score_objectives() computes the objective functions \(f_i(R)\) of eq. 7, each in \([0, 1]\):

Objective Definition What it rewards coverage answered sub-tasks ÷ all sub-tasks in the plan (skipped ones count as unanswered); a sub-task is answered when a non-refused response with at least one claim exists investigating every facet of the question density min(1, fused claims ÷ (non-refused tokens ÷ 60)) distinct information per token, the paper's bits-per-token notion agreement mean pairwise Jaccard overlap of the source ids cited by the non-refused responses; 1.0 with a single response, 0.0 with none independent responses converging on the same records recency mean time weight (from the memory's decay policy) of every source cited by the fused claims answers built on current records cost clip(1 − spent ÷ total_budget, 0, 1) budget left over

"Spent" is the sum of the executed sub-tasks' costs, plus half a sub-task's cost for every refinement re-run.

docs.title: The objective (eq. 7)
docs.text:
The paper formulates response optimisation as a weighted sum under epsilon constraints:

\[\max_{R}\; J(R) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} w_i f_i(R) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad f_j(R) \geq \epsilon_j,\ \forall j\]

weighted_sum(obj, weights, constraints) returns \(J\) normalised by the sum of the weights, whether every constraint holds, and the list of violated objectives. Weights \(w_i\) are ControllerPolicy.objectives and thresholds \(\epsilon_j\) are ControllerPolicy.constraints; both are validated against the five objective names.

from poincare_orchestra import ControllerPolicy, weighted_sum

policy = ControllerPolicy()
print(policy.objectives, policy.constraints)
print(
    weighted_sum(
        {"coverage": 0.67, "density": 1.0, "agreement": 0.0, "recency": 1.0, "cost": 0.2},
        policy.objectives,
        policy.constraints,
    )
)
print(
    weighted_sum(
        {"coverage": 0.33, "density": 0.1, "agreement": 1.0, "recency": 1.0, "cost": 0.9},
        policy.objectives,
        policy.constraints,
    )
)

{'coverage': 0.4, 'density': 0.2, 'agreement': 0.1, 'recency': 0.15, 'cost': 0.15} {'coverage': 0.5, 'density': 0.2}
(0.648, True, [])
(0.537, False, ['coverage', 'density'])

The second response has a respectable \(J\) but violates both constraints: a cheap, agreeing answer that covers a third of the question is not acceptable, which is what the epsilon constraints are for.

docs.title: Uncertainty
docs.text: SynthesisResult.uncertainty is a proxy in \([0, 1]\): \(1 - \bar{c}\,(1 - r)\) where \(\bar{c}\) is the mean confidence of the fused claims and \(r\) the share of refused responses; with no claims at all it is 1.0. Cross-provider disagreement is reported separately as the agreement objective rather than folded in, so the two signals stay interpretable.

docs.title: End to end
docs.text:
synthesize() takes the plan, the responses, the memory's time weights, the policy's weights and constraints, and the budget position:

from poincare_orchestra import ControllerPolicy, Plan, SubTask, synthesize

plan = Plan(
    query="What is the current API rate limit?",
    intent="factual",
    complexity=0.3,
    subtasks=[
        SubTask(id="q1", question="rate limit (focus: api)"),
        SubTask(id="q2", question="rate limit (focus: tickets)"),
        SubTask(id="q3", question="rate limit (focus: storage)"),
    ],
)
policy = ControllerPolicy()
result = synthesize(
    plan,
    responses,
    {"rate_new": 1.0, "rel24": 0.8, "auth": 1.0},
    policy.objectives,
    policy.constraints,
    spent=2.5,
    budget=6.0,
)
print({k: round(v, 3) for k, v in result.objective_scores.items()})
print(round(result.weighted_score, 3), result.constraints_met, result.violated, round(result.uncertainty, 3))
print(result.answer)

0.727 True [] 0.15
Synthesis across 2 perspective(s): tier1, tier2.
- (0.90) API rate limit is 250 requests per second [rate_new, rel24]
- (0.80) Tokens expire after 60 minutes [auth]
Open sub-questions: rate limit (focus: storage)

Coverage is 2/3 because q3 has no response. Agreement is the Jaccard overlap of the two responses' sources lists, {rate_new} and {rate_new, rel24, auth}: 1/3. Recency is the mean weight of the records the fused claims cite (1.0, 0.8, 1.0). Cost is 1 − 2.5/6.0. With the default weights, J = 0.4·0.667 + 0.2·1.0 + 0.1·0.333 + 0.15·0.933 + 0.15·0.583 ≈ 0.727, both constraints hold, and uncertainty is 1 − 0.85 (the mean fused confidence) with no refusals. The composed answer names the contributing roles, lists the fused claims with their supporting record ids, and ends with the open sub-questions.

docs.title: Refinement
docs.text:
After the first synthesis, Orchestrator.run loops while constraints_met is false and fewer than policy.refine_rounds rounds have run:

  1. InvestmentScheduler.reinvest measures each response's yield (distinct claims per 100 tokens) and splits the remaining budget over the lower-yielding half of the sub-tasks.
  2. Those sub-tasks are executed again with the extra budget (a larger budget retrieves more context), and their previous responses are replaced.
  3. spent grows by half the sub-task's cost per re-run, and the synthesis is recomputed with refinements incremented.

If no budget remains the loop stops and the result reports the violated constraints. The refinement rounds appear in RunResult.trace (refine round 1: violated=[...] reinvest={...}) and in the INFO log.
